text: Dulcie Evonne September (20 August 1935 – 29 March 1988) was a South African anti-apartheid political activist who was assassinated in Paris, France, in 1988. The second eldest daughter of Jakobus and Susan September, she grew up in Gleemore, a suburb of Cape Town. While in Cape Town, she developed a strong awareness of apartheid’s injustices and became deeply involved in political activism, advocating for national liberation, democracy, and social justice. She began her primary education at Klipfontein Methodist Mission and later attended Athlone High School, where she experienced firsthand the segregation enforced by Bantu education laws, which became central to her political beliefs. Several of her teachers at Athlone High School were active in civic and political organizations, which helped shape her political consciousness. Though her formal schooling ended halfway through Standard Eight (Grade 10), she continued her education through night classes and passed her Standard Eight exams in 1952. In 1954, she enrolled at the Wesley Training School in Salt River to become a teacher and completed her Teacher’s Diploma in 1955 at Battswood Training College. She began teaching at City Mission School in Maitland and later at Bridgetown East Primary School in Athlone in 1956. In 1957, she joined the Cape Peninsula Students' Union (CPSU), affiliated with the Unity Movement of South Africa, where she met political allies such as Dr. Kenneth Abrahams, Ottilie Abrahams, Neville Alexander, Marcus Solomon, and Fikile Bam. She was also a member of the Athlone branch of the Teacher's League of South Africa (TLSA). After growing frustrated with TLSA, she joined the African Peoples' Democratic Union of Southern Africa (APDUSA) in 1960 and was elected to its finance committee. The APDUSA soon split due to internal conflict, and under the leadership of Dr. Kenneth Abrahams and Neville Alexander—both suspended in 1962—September and others formed the unofficial Caucus to resolve divisions. After the Sharpeville massacre, she and other activists adopted a militant stance. Under Neville Alexander’s direction, she co-founded the Yu Chi Chan Club (YCCC) in July 1962, inspired by the Chinese Communist Revolution and named after Chinese guerilla warfare, which was disbanded by the end of that year and replaced by the National Liberation Front (NLF) in January 1963. On 12 July 1963, security police raided both her and Neville Alexander’s homes, and when NLF materials were found, September was detained on 7 October 1963 and imprisoned without trial at Roeland Street Prison. She was charged under the Criminal Procedure Act for "conspiracy to commit acts of sabotage and incite acts of politically motivated violence," and after months of court proceedings, judgment was delivered on 15 April 1964. She was sentenced to five years in prison, during which she endured severe physical and psychological abuse. Along with Elizabeth van der Heyden, Doris van der Hayden, and Dorothy Alexander, she was transferred to Kroonstad, a facility for political prisoners, after authorities discovered they were radicalizing illiterate female prisoners. In March 1965, the Bloemfontein Appeal Court dismissed their appeals. She was released in April 1969 under a strict five-year banning order imposed by the Pretoria regime. The restrictions, under the Suppression of Communism Act of 1950, prohibited her from social gatherings, political activities, and teaching in South Africa, imposed a curfew, restricted her movement to “Bantu areas,” banned communication with other banned individuals, and limited visitors to medical personnel and her father—later changed to her sister and brother-in-law. In 1973, as her banning order neared expiration, she applied for a permanent departure permit after securing a position at Madeley College of Education in Staffordshire. She left South Africa on 19 December 1973. In London, she joined the Anti-Apartheid Movement, participated in rallies at South Africa House in Trafalgar Square, and later joined the International Defence and Aid Fund for Southern Africa. In 1976, she joined the African National Congress (ANC) and worked in the ANC Women's League, where she gained recognition for her work on women’s issues and helped welcome newly exiled South Africans. In 1979, during the International Year of the Child (IYC), she was elected chairperson of the IYC Committee of the ANC Women's Section in London. As an ANC representative, she attended conferences in Finland, Canada, and France and worked with the United Nations (UN), non-governmental organizations (NGOs), and the Women’s International Democratic Federation (WIDF) to promote children’s and women’s rights. In 1981, she was called to work full-time in the Regional Preparatory Committee (RPC) at ANC headquarters in Lusaka, where she was elected chairperson. By the end of 1983, she was appointed ANC Chief Representative in France, Switzerland, and Luxembourg, and underwent short military training in the Soviet Union. In this role, she campaigned for economic sanctions against the South African government. Between October 1986 and September 1987, she was involved in the Albertini Affair, an anti-apartheid campaign that ended with embarrassment for both South African and French governments, during which she campaigned for the release of Pierre Andre Albertini, a French national imprisoned by South Africa, and petitioned French President Francois Mitterrand to deny South Africa’s new ambassador, Hennie Geldenhuys, until Albertini was freed. By 1987, she had become a significant threat to the South African government, leading strong anti-apartheid campaigns in France, Switzerland, and Luxembourg and building strong alliances with anti-apartheid groups and left-wing politicians. On the morning of 29 March 1988, she was shot five times with a silenced .22 caliber rifle outside the ANC’s Paris office at 28, Rue des Petites-Écuries as she was opening the office after collecting mail. She was 52 years old. Her death sparked a strong public reaction in Paris, with more than 20,000 people gathering to mourn. The case remains unsolved, with speculation that South African hitmen were involved, possibly with French secret service collaboration. The French government concluded there was insufficient evidence to arrest suspects and closed the case after ten years. Before her assassination, she had been investigating illegal arms trafficking between France and South Africa. According to the Truth Commission Files, the motive may have been linked to her knowledge of illegal arms deals and possible nuclear collaboration between the French government and South African Armscor. Upon discovering this, she reportedly said she “feared for her life.” During her investigation, she reported her concerns to ANC superiors, who dismissed her. Some of her friends allege she reported being followed and threatened and requested protection from French authorities, which was denied. Charles Pasqua, the interior minister, denied these claims, stating she never made such a request. However, sources claim the French had intelligence that South Africa planned to kill her by December 1987, though this is officially denied. On the day after her murder, Alfred Nzo, secretary-general of the ANC, stated: "If ever there was a soft target, Dulcie September was one." Jean-Michel Jarre composed a song titled "September" for his 1988 Revolutions album, dedicated to her, which was performed at his Destination Docklands concert in October 1988 and included in the album recording Jarre Live (1989). Conceptual artist Hans Haacke created a 1989 installation titled "One Day, The Lions of Dulcie September Will Spout Water in Jubilation," modifying a defunct fountain in front of the Grande halle de la Villette in Paris as part of the Magiciens de la terre exhibition. Her short story "A Split Society – Fast Sounds on the Horizon" was included in the 1992 anthology Daughters of Africa, edited by Margaret Busby. The solo play Cold Case: Revisiting Dulcie September, written by Basil Appollis and Sylvia Vollenhoven, pays tribute to her and was performed at a French cultural festival in Paris, winning the inaugural Adelaide Tambo Award for Human Rights in the Arts. A book about her murder, Dulcie: Een Vrouw Die Haar Mond Moest Houden by Evelyn Groenink, was published in the Netherlands in 2001. A podcast titled They Killed Dulcie by Open Secrets and Sound Africa was released in March 2019. The 2021 documentary Murder in Paris, directed by Enver Samuel and edited by Nikki Comninos, explores her life and assassination. An online awareness campaign and petition for justice were launched using the hashtags “#justicefordulcie” and “#mercidulcie.” A 300-page graphic novel, Dulcie from Cape Town to Paris, published by Benoît Collombat and Grégory Mardon, revisits her murder investigation 30 years after her death. A square in the 10th arrondissement of Paris is named after her, officially inaugurated on 31 March 1998, with the inscription “Dulcie September Square: Representative of the African National Congress: Assassinated in Paris on 29 March 1988.” A street in Cléon, near Rouen, is named after her, as is a place in Nantes and a primary school in Évry-sur-Seine, as well as a middle school (collège) in Arcueil, near Paris. In August 2010, the first Dulcie September Memorial Lecture took place at the University of the Western Cape’s Centre for Humanities Research, and the Dulcie September Fellowship Awards in the Humanities and Social Sciences were launched, featuring speakers including Barbara Masekela and Margaret Busby. In October 2011, Staffordshire University Students' Union renamed their boardroom the "September Room" and erected a plaque in her memory. She was a former student of Madeley College of Education, one of the founding colleges of North Staffordshire Polytechnic. In 2013, the Athlone Civic Centre was renamed the Dulcie September Civic Centre. In Amsterdam, a road in the Transvaalbuurt is named Dulcie Septemberpad, and other buildings and streets in the neighborhood bear the names of prominent South Africans, including Steve Bikoplein, Nelson Mandela School, and Retiefstraat.
